brief: A soldering station for my bench: a holder for the iron while it is switched on and hot, plus two bins for solder and spare tips.

requirements.requirement: Holder for the soldering iron while it is switched on and hot
requirements.evidence: No iron holder or iron prop exists in the catalog. Built a cradle: bin piece (0,-1,0) with hex-bin-full-cup (mug ring seat) on a piece cell, bolted to the base with a joint bolt. It is a seat, not a purpose-made iron stand, and the configurator cannot verify heat resistance of the printed material; the user must confirm the material and fit for a hot iron.
bin:0,0,0~hex-bin-full (full-depth tray) on piece (0,0,0), locked with joint bolt. Mesh clear.
bin:1,0,0~hex-bin-full (full-depth tray) on piece (1,0,0), joined to the solder bin cell by a joint bolt. Mesh clear.

requirements.requirement: Built for a bench, with two bins and the iron holder as one station
requirements.evidence: Three piece cells in a row/corner: (0,0),(1,0),(0,-1); check_build reports meshClash clear and no rule errors.

finish.summary: Soldering station built: two full-depth bins (solder at 0,0; spare tips at 1,0) on bolted base cells, plus a mug-ring bin at 0,-1 as the iron cradle. Mesh clear, no errors. The iron holder is only a partial answer: no purpose-made iron holder exists, and heat resistance of the chosen material is unverifiable here.

lines.label: M6 x 25 socket head screw, ISO 4762

notes: Tighten every M6 to 2 N.m: HAND TOOLS ONLY, never a cordless driver. These bolts clamp printed PETG, not metal: at the bolt's own 10.4 N.m rating the head crushes the plastic under it and the joint fails silently, looking tight while holding nothing. Snug, then a nudge. Re-check the bolts after the first few weeks: PETG relaxes under load and the clamp will have eased.
